question: Can I read, run and fix code an AI wrote?
learn: Read Python: variables, functions, loops, dictionaries (key-value lookups), classes (bundles of data and functions), exceptions (how code signals failure)
Write small scripts unaided first, so you can tell when an agent (AI that writes and runs code) is wrong
Use the terminal: run programs, move files, set up virtual environments (per-project package installs)
Use Git (version history for code): commit, branch, read a diff (what changed), undo
Debug by method: reproduce, shrink the case, guess, test the guess with logs or a debugger (tool that pauses running code)
Read stack traces (the error's trail through the code), and explain every line an agent hands you
drop: Memorising syntax and library calls: agents and docs supply them, and a 2026 curriculum paper ranks this as devalued
Manual memory work in C: CS50 still teaches it, but the concept is enough and belongs in A4
Learning several languages: Python plus SQL covers this goal, and language choice matters less now
Editor tricks and typing speed: agents write most first drafts, so reading speed counts for more
head_start: Basic SQL gives you precise requests and checking a result against what you expected. You rarely write Python, so writing and debugging start near zero.
judge_check: Situation: An agent-written Python script turns a 2-million-row export into a weekly revenue table and prints 'Success' on every run. This week's total jumped 12% with no business reason. Check: (1) Does a broad exception handler (code that catches any error and carries on) make 'Success' meaningless? (2) Do row counts jump after a join, meaning duplicate keys are inflating revenue? (3) What does the Git diff show changed since the last good run, including package versions?
understand_check: Build a 100-line script with an agent that downloads a CSV, cleans it and loads it into SQLite (a one-file database), with at least five Git commits. Have a second agent plant a bug without telling you where, then find it using only logs or a debugger, with no AI explaining it. Finish by walking through every function aloud.

question: Can I state exactly what must be true, and spot exceptions?
learn: And, or, not, if-then, and how to negate a claim correctly
'For all' versus 'there exists': one counterexample kills a 'for all' claim
Preconditions and postconditions (what must hold before and after code runs)
Invariants (facts that must stay true throughout), such as 'refunds never exceed payments'
Induction (if each step preserves a fact, it always holds) as the idea behind loops: read it, don't write it
Property-based tests (checking a rule against many generated inputs) as the everyday stand-in for proof
drop: Writing formal proofs by hand: an exam skill; you need the reasoning, and Kleppmann expects AI to make the mechanics far cheaper
Number theory and RSA (a public-key encryption method) mathematics: for cryptographers; use vetted libraries
Automata and computability theory (what abstract machines can compute): taught in CS103 and CS 70, but rarely changes a product decision
Proof assistants such as Lean or Dafny (tools that machine-check proofs): promising, but still a forecast for mainstream work, and writing the specification stays the hard part
head_start: SQL WHERE clauses are already and/or/not logic, including the trap that NULL (a missing value) breaks simple true/false thinking. Basic statistics adds reasoning from stated assumptions.
judge_check: Situation: An AI agent writes a refund rule: refund if the order is under 30 days old and not final-sale. All 20 example tests pass, and product says customers must never get back more than they paid. Check: (1) Boundaries: exactly day 30, time zones, and a blank final-sale field. (2) The invariant: is 'total refunds never exceed amount paid' tested across generated orders, not just 20 examples? (3) The counterexample: can two partial refunds arriving together break it?
understand_check: Take a business rule you know, such as commission or refunds. Write its preconditions, postconditions and two invariants on one page, find two counterexamples to a first draft, then have an agent write a property-based test with Hypothesis (a Python testing library) that catches one. Explain why that test beats 20 examples yet still isn't a proof.

question: How will this work slow down as the data grows?
learn: Growth rates (big-O, how cost rises with data size): constant, logarithmic, linear, n log n, squared
Back-of-envelope scaling: predict 5 million rows from a test on 1,000
Core structures by what they make fast: arrays, hash tables (instant lookup by key), trees, queues, graphs (networks of linked items)
Sorting and binary search (halving a sorted list repeatedly), and why a database index (a sorted lookup structure) changes the cost
Spotting hidden repeated work: nested loops, one database query per row
Trade-offs: caching (keeping answers for reuse) and vector indexes (fast similarity search that may miss some matches)
drop: Hand-coding balanced trees or graph algorithms: libraries and agents do it; know when each applies
Interview puzzle drilling: irrelevant to this goal, and Canva replaced its fundamentals screen because AI solves such questions
Solving recurrences and amortised-cost proofs (formal running-time maths): a rough growth class is enough to judge
Dynamic programming techniques (building answers from stored sub-answers): recognise the name, then ask an agent
head_start: Warehouse work probably gave you some feel for which scans and joins get expensive. The vocabulary for predicting growth is new.
judge_check: Situation: An AI agent builds a duplicate-customer finder that fuzzy-matches (compares approximately) each record against every other, and it takes 8 seconds on a 1,000-row sample. Production has 5 million rows. Check: (1) Growth: comparing all pairs is squared, so 5,000 times the rows means 25 million times the work, about six years on this setup. (2) Can a cheap key such as postcode narrow the candidates first, and how many true duplicates would that miss? (3) Does it call a database or model once per pair, where per-call cost dwarfs the loop itself?
understand_check: With an agent writing the code, time three tasks at 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 rows: list versus dictionary lookup, nested-loop join versus hash join (matching through a lookup table), and a query before and after adding an index. Predict the 10 million result from your chart before running it, then explain any miss.

question: What actually happens on the machine when code runs?
learn: The speed ladder: CPU cache (tiny fast memory on the processor), main memory, disk and network each differ by orders of magnitude
Processes and threads (separate programs versus parallel paths sharing memory), and what the operating system does
Memory limits: why big jobs get killed, and streaming data versus loading it all
Concurrency: race conditions (results depend on timing), locks (one-at-a-time access), deadlocks (each side waiting on the other forever), waiting on slow operations without stalling
Measure before optimising: elapsed versus CPU time, profilers (tools showing where time goes)
Why GPUs (chips doing many simple sums at once) dominate language-model work
drop: Assembly language (human-readable machine instructions): compilers (code-to-machine translators) and agents handle it, and it rarely changes a product call
Logic gates and CPU pipelines (how processors are physically built): Berkeley CS 61C teaches them, but they don't help you judge software
Writing kernels, page tables or schedulers (operating system internals): know what they do, not how to build them
Manual memory allocation in C: Python manages it; the idea of limited memory is what matters
judge_check: Situation: A nightly Python job loads a 40 GB file on a 32 GB machine, and an agent (AI that writes and runs code) 'fixed' its crashes with eight threads and an automatic retry. It now dies at random hours, and some totals come out wrong. Check: (1) Is the file bigger than memory? Threads don't add memory. (2) Can threads overwrite each other's shared total? (3) Does a rerun after a partial failure count rows twice?
understand_check: Have an agent write a script that sums a large file three ways: load all of it, stream it, and split it across processes. Measure time and peak memory for each and explain the differences. Then build a two-thread counter that reads, pauses and writes back, show it losing updates, fix it with a lock, and say why the fix works.

question: How do programs talk to each other and keep data safely?
learn: HTTP (the web's request-response format), status codes, JSON (a text data format); every language-model API (programmatic interface) call uses them
One line each on DNS (name lookup), TCP (reliable delivery) and TLS (encryption)
Network failure: timeouts, retries, idempotency (repeating a request does no extra harm)
Transactions (all-or-nothing changes) and what they do and don't promise
Live databases versus warehouses: indexes (sorted lookups that find rows fast), query plans (how the database will run a query), why analytics shouldn't hit live tables
Choosing storage: Postgres (popular open-source database) first, then object stores (cheap file buckets), caches (fast copies of frequent answers), vector indexes (search by similarity)
drop: Packet routing such as BGP (how networks share routes): cloud providers handle it, and app builders rarely touch it
Building database internals like buffer pools (memory caches for disk pages): CMU 15-445's projects go there; using a database needs only the concepts
Socket programming (hand-written network connections): libraries and agents cover it
Touring every NoSQL (non-relational) product: Postgres now covers many of their jobs, and product names churn
head_start: Your biggest overlap. Basic SQL and warehousing give you tables, keys and joins. New ground is the live side: transactions, many simultaneous writers, and indexes tuned for single-row lookups.
judge_check: Situation: An app calls a payment API, then writes the order to Postgres, and AI-written code retries whenever the call times out. Customers report double charges, and checkout has slowed since a new dashboard began reading the orders table. Check: (1) Is there an idempotency key (a unique ID that marks a retry as the same request), since a timeout doesn't mean the charge failed? (2) What happens if the charge succeeds and the database write fails? (3) Should the dashboard's big scans move to a read replica (a read-only copy) or the warehouse?
understand_check: With an agent, build a two-table app behind one web endpoint (a URL that does one job), and call it with curl (a command-line web client) so you can read the status code and JSON. Load a million rows and compare query plans before and after an index. Then simulate a timeout that double-charges, and fix it with an idempotency key, a unique constraint (a database rule forbidding duplicates) and a transaction.

question: How is code structured and checked so change stays safe?
learn: Modules and interfaces (parts that hide their inner workings) so changes stay local
Specifications: write expected behaviour down before code exists
Test types: unit (one part), integration (parts together), regression (stops old bugs returning), property-based (rules across generated inputs)
Test quality: would it fail if the code were wrong? Mutation testing (planting bugs on purpose) answers this
Automatic checks: types (declared kinds of data, checked by tools), linters (bug and style scanners), CI (checks run on every change)
Code review and small changes: read each diff (what changed), reject what you can't explain
drop: Memorising named design patterns: agents recall them, and Thoughtworks' 2026 Radar advises holding principles over patterns
Chasing 100% coverage (share of lines tests touch): MIT warns against over-focusing on it, since it doesn't show the checks mean anything
Formatting and style rules: formatters and linters enforce them automatically
Spec-as-source workflows (people edit only specs, code is generated): Böckeler warns they risk rigidity plus unpredictability

judge_check: Situation: An agent (AI that writes and runs code) delivers a 900-line pull request (a proposed code change) for a discount feature, with 40 new tests, all passing, and coverage up to 95%. (2) Did a person approve a written statement of expected behaviour? (3) Is discount logic in one module, or scattered across checkout so the next change touches everything?
understand_check: Write a one-page spec for a small feature. Have an agent write failing tests first, confirm they fail, then implement. question: How does code reach users and stay safe and running?
learn: Path to production: separate test and live environments, CI/CD (automatic test and release), secrets (passwords and keys) kept out of code
Rollbacks and backups you have actually tried
Operating: logs, metrics, alerts, who gets paged, postmortems (blame-free incident write-ups)
Web security baseline: broken access control, injection (input run as commands), misconfiguration; anything in the browser is public
Supply chain: dependencies (other people's code you rely on), lockfiles (pinned versions), and package names AI invents
Privacy and agents: collect less, watch logs and prompts, least privilege (minimum access), prompt injection (hidden instructions in content)
drop: Writing Kubernetes configuration (a system for running many packaged apps): managed hosts cover small systems; know what it's for
Cryptography maths: use TLS (standard web encryption) and vetted libraries, and never write your own
Memory-corruption exploits and assembly attacks: Berkeley CS 161 teaches them, but memory-safe languages like Python avoid most of this class
Compliance certificate detail such as SOC 2 (an audit standard): get help when a customer asks; learn the principles first
judge_check: Situation: A business team ships a customer-lookup tool from an AI app builder, with a hosted database and a public web page. It demoed well, and nobody has a rollback or on-call (who responds to incidents) plan. Check: (1) Access: are rules enforced in the database, or can anyone using the key shipped in the page read every row? Apps built on Lovable, an AI app builder, were exposed this way. (2) Secrets and personal data: any API keys (passwords for services) in browser code, or customer details in logs and prompts? (3) Recovery: is test separated from live, has a restore from backup actually been run, and who gets alerted?
understand_check: Deploy the B1 app through an automated pipeline with secrets in environment variables (settings supplied at run time), structured logs, one real alert and a rollback you have performed. Try to read another user's record and show it fails, run a dependency audit (a scan for known-vulnerable packages), and write one page on who can see what. Then retell Cloudflare's November 2025 outage in five sentences of your own.

question: What shape should this product and its data flow take?
learn: Estimating load: users, requests, data size and cost, before choosing anything
Scaling moves in order: better queries, caching, read replicas (read-only copies), then sharding (splitting data across machines)
Failure thinking: what breaks first, single points of failure, consistency (everyone sees the same data) versus availability (the system keeps answering)
Data pipelines: batch versus streaming (scheduled bulk runs versus continuous flow), data lakes (cheap raw storage), data quality and ownership
ML data flow: training versus serving data, versioning, drift (live data moving away from training data)
AI product anatomy: retrieval (fetching documents), tools (functions the model can use), evals (tests for AI output), guardrails (blocks on bad input or output), cost and speed budgets
drop: Implementing consensus such as Raft (how machines agree on one answer): MIT 6.5840 builds it; you need only why it exists
Memorised 'design Twitter' interview answers: they teach shapes without the habit of estimating your own load
Microservices (many small separate services) and multi-region (copies across geographies) by default: OpenAI reports one write database plus about 50 read copies at 800 million users
Comparing tool brands, such as Kafka (a streaming message system) and its rivals: products churn; learn what job each category does
head_start: Warehousing gives you a starting sense of data modeling and why large scans cost money. New ground is live serving: many users at once, failures mid-request, and response time.
judge_check: Situation: A team plans an internal assistant over 2 million support documents for 200 staff, at about two questions a minute. The design has microservices, Kafka, a standalone vector database (a store for similarity search) and multi-region sharding from day one. Check: (1) Load: two questions a minute is tiny, so would one Postgres (open-source database) with a vector index do? (2) The real risks: can staff retrieve only documents they may see, and how stale is the index? (3) Is there an eval set showing retrieval works, plus a per-question cost and a plan for provider outages?
understand_check: Write a two-page design for that assistant at 5,000 staff: estimate traffic, storage and token (model billing unit) costs, draw the flow from ingest to answer to logging, name the first bottleneck and top three failure modes, and list what you won't build yet. Ask an agent to attack it, then defend or change each point.

question: Why do language models behave, fail and cost as they do?
learn: Tokens (the chunks models read), embeddings (meaning as numbers), the context window (how much a model can see at once)
Attention and transformers (the design behind LLMs, large language models) at diagram level
Pretraining on text, then post-training on human preferences and rewards, which creates assistant behaviour
Why they fail: guessing when unsure, random sampling, recall fading as context grows
What isn't proof: shown reasoning and public benchmarks don't establish correctness on your task
Economics: per-token pricing, GPU (parallel maths chip) serving, prompt caching (reusing recent input cheaply), small versus large models
drop: Implementing GPU kernels (low-level chip code) or distributed training (across many machines): CS336 builds these for future model makers; product work rarely needs them
Deriving backpropagation (how training computes corrections) by hand: the idea from basic ML is enough
Older sequence models such as RNNs and LSTMs (pre-transformer designs): a paragraph of history will do

head_start: Basic ML gives you training versus test data, loss, overfitting and features. Basic statistics gives you sampling and probability, which is what an LLM outputs. What's new is scale and architecture.
judge_check: Situation: A vendor demos a policy assistant that feeds your whole 400-page manual to the model on every question and shows its reasoning steps as proof of accuracy. Its slide claims 94% on a public benchmark. Check: (1) Context and cost: roughly 250,000 tokens per question raises the bill and may blur recall, so why not retrieve only the relevant pages? (2) Shown reasoning isn't evidence: Anthropic found models disclosed hints they had used only 25% to 39% of the time. (3) Test on your own questions, including ones the manual can't answer: does it admit ignorance or guess?
understand_check: Read and run Karpathy's 200-line microgpt with an agent as tutor. Change the block size (its context length) and the temperature (how random sampling is), predict each effect first, then check. Then explain to a colleague, without notes: tokenisation, attention, why models hallucinate (state false things confidently), what post-training changes, and what one chat turn costs at a stated price.

notes: Two skills share this name: directing coding agents, and evaluating AI features in a product. Move the second to the proposed AI product topic if B4 is split. Productivity evidence is unsettled: METR's early-2025 trial found 19% slower, while its late-2025 rerun shows 18% and 4% faster, with intervals crossing zero and admitted selection bias. Checking pays either way. In Stack Overflow's 2026 survey, 48% trust AI when output is easy to verify and 6.6% for important decisions. Anthropic's trial links delegation to quiz scores under 40% and asking for explanations to 65% or more, which is also a study rule for this learner. Several sources sell AI tools, and I am an Anthropic model citing Anthropic, so weigh those accordingly. CS146S expects strong programming (CS111/CS161 level), so use it as a syllabus.
